candidates.label: Mount Gerizim
candidates.support: Wikidata's point for Mount Gerizim is corroborated by OpenBible.info's independently recorded point for the same mountain, overlooking Nablus (ancient Shechem) and Jacob's Well. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the mountain's height as 2,849 feet and locates it immediately south of the pass through which the main road from the coast to the Jordan Valley runs.

summary.text: Mount Gerizim stands south of the pass where the town of Shechem, and later Nablus, lies, facing Mount Ebal across the valley. John's Gospel does not name the mountain, but records a Samaritan woman telling Jesus at Jacob's well, "Our fathers worshiped in this mountain," to which Jesus replies that true worshipers will worship the Father "neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Gerizim as "this mountain" of the conversation, since the well lies almost beneath its cliffs.

history.text: Deuteronomy directs that after Israel entered the land, blessings were to be pronounced from Mount Gerizim and curses from Mount Ebal, a ceremony Joshua is recorded as carrying out, with the Levites and the ark stationed in the valley between the two mountains.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, citing the first-century Jewish historian Josephus, records that a temple was built on Gerizim around 432 BC, rivaling the Temple in Jerusalem, after a dispute over the marriage of a high-priestly family member to the daughter of Sanballat the Horonite; this schism, it notes, lies behind the continuing division between Jews and Samaritans, who still worship separately today. The Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple on the mountain around 110 BC. Samaritans maintain their own community and continue to celebrate the Passover on the mountain each year.

scripture.textWEB: Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, and you Jews say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”
Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither in this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.

otConnections.note: Moses instructs that the blessing be set on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal once Israel enters the land.
Six tribes are named to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people when this command is carried out.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
